subject: Economy
sub_topic: Exchange rate regimes — fixed, flexible, managed float

concepts.name: Fixed Exchange Rate System: Mechanics and Maintenance
key_dimensions: How a central bank pegs currency to a reference (gold, USD, basket) and the intervention mechanism
Difference between 'hard peg' (currency board, dollarization) vs 'soft peg' (adjustable peg, crawling peg)
Role of foreign exchange reserves in defending the peg — when reserves run out (balance of payments crisis)
UPSC trap: Fixed rate does NOT mean exchange rate never changes — it can be officially devalued/revalued

concepts.name: Devaluation vs Depreciation: Conceptual Distinction and Effects
key_dimensions: Devaluation = deliberate government/central bank policy decision (fixed regime); Depreciation = market-driven fall (flexible regime)
Revaluation vs Appreciation — the symmetric upward movements and which regime each belongs to
Effects on exports, imports, current account, inflation (imported inflation), and debt servicing
UPSC trap: Devaluation improves trade balance only if Marshall-Lerner condition is satisfied; J-curve effect in the short run

concepts.name: Marshall-Lerner Condition and the J-Curve Effect
key_dimensions: Marshall-Lerner condition: trade balance improves after depreciation only if sum of price elasticities of exports and imports > 1
J-curve: short-run worsening of trade balance after depreciation before long-run improvement — why contracts are pre-committed
Factors determining elasticity: nature of goods (luxury vs necessity), availability of substitutes, time horizon
UPSC trap: In the short run, depreciation can WORSEN the current account — counterintuitive but examinable

concepts.name: Flexible (Freely Floating) Exchange Rate System
key_dimensions: Rate determined purely by demand and supply of currency in forex market — no central bank intervention
Automatic adjustment mechanism: BOP deficit → currency depreciates → exports rise, imports fall → BOP corrects
Advantages: monetary policy autonomy, no need for large reserves, automatic stabilizer
UPSC trap: Pure free float is theoretical; virtually no country operates a completely free float — always some intervention

concepts.name: Managed Float (Dirty Float): India's Exchange Rate Regime
key_dimensions: Definition: exchange rate primarily market-determined but RBI intervenes to prevent excessive volatility — neither fixed nor free
India officially follows 'managed float with no predetermined target' since 1993 (post-Liberalization)
RBI tools: buying/selling USD in forex market, MSS (Market Stabilization Scheme), interest rate signaling
UPSC trap: RBI does NOT target a specific exchange rate level — it targets 'orderly market conditions'; distinction from a peg

concepts.name: The Impossible Trinity (Trilemma) of International Finance
key_dimensions: A country cannot simultaneously have: (1) fixed exchange rate, (2) free capital flows, (3) independent monetary policy
Only two of the three can be achieved at once — each corner of the trilemma triangle with real-world examples
China's choice: fixed rate + monetary autonomy → capital controls; Eurozone: fixed rate + free capital → lost monetary policy
India's position: managed float + partial capital controls → retains some monetary autonomy (middle path)
UPSC trap: The trilemma is attributed to Mundell-Fleming model — knowing the theorists matters for MCQs

concepts.name: Purchasing Power Parity (PPP): Theory and Limitations
key_dimensions: Absolute PPP: exchange rate should equalize price levels across countries (Law of One Price)
Relative PPP: exchange rate changes reflect inflation differentials between countries
Why PPP exchange rate differs from market exchange rate: non-tradables, transport costs, trade barriers, Balassa-Samuelson effect
UPSC trap: World Bank/IMF use PPP-adjusted GDP for cross-country comparisons — India's GDP rank changes significantly under PPP vs nominal

concepts.name: Nominal vs Real Effective Exchange Rate (NEER and REER)
key_dimensions: NEER: weighted average of bilateral nominal exchange rates against a basket of currencies (trade-weighted)
REER: NEER adjusted for relative inflation differentials — measures actual competitiveness
REER > 100 means currency is overvalued (exports become less competitive); REER < 100 means undervalued
RBI publishes 6-currency and 36-currency REER indices — used to assess India's export competitiveness
UPSC trap: A currency can nominally depreciate but still be overvalued in real terms if domestic inflation is very high

concepts.name: Currency Board Arrangement: Extreme Fixed Regime
key_dimensions: 100% backing of domestic currency by foreign reserve — monetary base fully backed, central bank has no discretion
Examples: Hong Kong (pegged to USD since 1983), Estonia (before Euro), Argentina 1991-2002
Eliminates monetary policy autonomy completely — cannot act as lender of last resort
UPSC trap: Currency board is NOT the same as dollarization — country retains its own currency but fully backed; dollarization = adopting another country's currency

concepts.name: Speculative Attacks and Currency Crisis
key_dimensions: Mechanism: when a peg is seen as unsustainable, speculators short-sell the currency forcing reserves to deplete and peg to collapse
First-generation models (Krugman): fiscal deficits + fixed rate = inevitable collapse
Second-generation models (Obstfeld): self-fulfilling crises — even sustainable pegs can collapse if everyone expects collapse
Real-world examples: 1992 UK ERM crisis (Soros), 1997 Asian financial crisis (Thailand Baht), 1991 India forex crisis
UPSC trap: India's 1991 crisis was a BOP crisis + reserve crisis leading to devaluation — distinct from a speculative attack but often confused

concepts.name: India's Exchange Rate History: From Fixed to Managed Float
key_dimensions: Pre-1991: fixed/pegged regime, overvalued rupee, administered by RBI under government direction
1991: Rupee devalued in two tranches (July 1-3) by ~18-19% as part of crisis response
1992-93: Liberalized Exchange Rate Management System (LERMS) — dual exchange rate transition mechanism
1993: Unified exchange rate — move to market-determined (managed float) system; current account convertibility followed
UPSC trap: India has current account convertibility but NOT full capital account convertibility — distinction is critical

concepts.name: Current Account vs Capital Account Convertibility
key_dimensions: Current account convertibility: freedom to convert currency for trade in goods, services, income — India has this since 1994
Capital account convertibility (CAC): freedom to convert for financial assets — India has PARTIAL CAC with controls on FDI/FPI limits
Tarapore Committee (1997 and 2006): recommended preconditions for full CAC — fiscal consolidation, low inflation, strong banking sector
UPSC trap: FDI is more liberalized than FPI in terms of capital controls; ECB (External Commercial Borrowings) have separate limits — not full CAC

concepts.name: Foreign Exchange Reserves: Composition, Adequacy Measures
key_dimensions: Components: foreign currency assets (largest), gold, SDRs, reserve tranche with IMF
Adequacy measures: Guidotti-Greenspan rule (reserves ≥ one year of external debt), import cover (3 months minimum), Wijnholds-Kapteyn metric
India's reserve management: RBI Act — reserves invested in safe, liquid foreign assets (US Treasuries, gold)
UPSC trap: SDRs are NOT a currency but an international reserve asset/claim on IMF member currencies — often confused as a separate currency

concepts.name: Special Drawing Rights (SDRs): Nature and Role
key_dimensions: SDR is an international reserve asset created by IMF in 1969 to supplement official reserves — not a currency
SDR basket composition (2022 review): USD, Euro, CNY, JPY, GBP — Chinese Yuan added in 2016
SDR allocations by IMF: COVID-19 special allocation of SDR 456 billion in August 2021 (largest ever)
UPSC trap: SDR interest rate is a weighted average of short-term government bond rates of basket currencies — NOT the same as IMF lending rate

concepts.name: Sterilization of Forex Interventions
key_dimensions: When RBI buys USD (to prevent rupee appreciation), it injects rupees → excess liquidity → inflationary pressure
Sterilization: RBI simultaneously sells government securities (open market operations) to absorb excess rupees
Market Stabilization Scheme (MSS): special government securities issued specifically for sterilization — off regular fiscal account
UPSC trap: Sterilization is not perfect — if complete, RBI bears the cost of holding low-yield USD assets vs higher-yield domestic assets (quasi-fiscal cost)

concepts.name: Carry Trade and Exchange Rate Volatility
key_dimensions: Carry trade: borrowing in low-interest-rate currency (e.g., JPY) and investing in high-interest-rate currency (e.g., INR) for profit
Effect on exchange rates: carry trade inflows appreciate the high-yield currency; sudden unwinding causes sharp depreciation
Uncovered Interest Rate Parity (UIP): theory says carry trade profits should be zero (exchange rate adjusts) — but empirically it persists
UPSC trap: Carry trade is a major source of capital flow volatility for emerging markets like India — linked to Fed rate decisions and 'taper tantrum'

concepts.name: Dutch Disease: Exchange Rate and Resource Exports
key_dimensions: Phenomenon where large natural resource exports (or capital inflows) cause currency appreciation, making manufacturing uncompetitive
Named after Netherlands' natural gas discovery in 1960s that hurt Dutch manufacturing exports
Two channels: spending effect (higher incomes raise demand for non-tradables) and resource movement effect (labor shifts to resource sector)
UPSC trap: Dutch Disease can also be triggered by large remittance inflows or aid inflows — not just resource exports; relevant for India's remittance discussion

concepts.name: Currency Manipulation: Criteria and Global Implications
key_dimensions: US Treasury criteria for labeling a country a 'currency manipulator': large bilateral surplus with US, large current account surplus (>3% GDP), persistent one-sided forex intervention (>2% GDP)
China labeled currency manipulator in 2019 (briefly); India on 'monitoring list' multiple times
WTO rules on currency: no explicit prohibition but IMF Article IV obliges members not to manipulate for unfair competitive advantage
UPSC trap: Being on the US monitoring list does NOT mean formal 'manipulator' designation — there are two separate thresholds; India has been on the watch list but not designated

concepts.name: Exchange Rate Pass-Through to Inflation
key_dimensions: Pass-through: extent to which exchange rate depreciation translates into higher domestic prices (import price inflation)
Complete pass-through vs incomplete pass-through — depends on market structure, pricing power, import share in consumption basket
India: high pass-through for crude oil (since oil is dollar-denominated and India imports ~85% of needs) → depreciation raises fuel prices
UPSC trap: RBI considers exchange rate pass-through in inflation forecasting; rupee depreciation is an UPSIDE risk to inflation — relevant for monetary policy decisions

concepts.name: Optimum Currency Area (OCA) Theory and Its Relevance to Regional Integration
key_dimensions: Mundell's OCA theory: a group of countries benefits from a common currency if they have labor mobility, capital mobility, similar business cycles, fiscal transfers
Eurozone as a test case: failed OCA criteria (limited labor mobility, no fiscal union) — explains Eurozone debt crisis asymmetric impact
SACEP/SAARC monetary integration: why South Asian common currency is unlikely — divergent inflation, different trade structures, political tensions
UPSC trap: Joining a currency union = giving up exchange rate as adjustment tool — countries must rely on internal devaluation (wage/price cuts) which is politically difficult; Greece example
